tone_statements.citation: Odden, David. 1995. Tone: African languages. In John A. Goldsmith (ed.), The Handbook of Phonological Theory, 444-475. Oxford & Cambridge, MA: Blackwell.
tone_statements.quote: Kanakuru (Newman 1974) provides better evidence for right-to-left linking. Stems either have the tone pattern HL or LH subject to the condition that if the stem begins with a voiced stop the stem selects the pattern HL, and if the initial is voiceless, the pattern LH is selected. Stems with an initial vowel or sonorant unpredictably select either HL or LH. ... In trisyllabic words, the first two syllables always bear the first tone of the melody, and the last vowel alone bears the final tone of the melody. In short, the distribution of tones in Kanakuru is the mirror image of Mende.
tone_statements.locator: sec. 3, between ex. (45) and (46) and the paragraph after (46); Blackwell Reference Online print-out pp. 16-17 of 29; second passage (consonant types, 'Certain peculiar cases remain unexplained..') on print-out p. 9; print edition pp. 444-475
tone_statements.summary: 2 levels H, L (+ downstep from floating L, derived HL fall); verb-stem melody HL/LH selected by initial consonant (voiced stop -> HL, voiceless -> LH); right-to-left association (Odden after Newman 1974).

sources.citation: Newman, Paul. 1981. Syllable weight and tone. Linguistic Inquiry 12(4): 670-673.
sources.note: Kanakuru, Bole and Hausa are all tonal; Kanakuru -ak verbal-noun tone determined by syllable weight (citing Newman 1974); syllable weight 'like stress—which also does not normally cooccur with distinctive tone—is rhythmic (metrical)'. Nothing on stress placement in Kanakuru.

Nouns, adjectives and adverbs have either H or HL underlying tones, while verbs are postulated to have either HL or LH underlying tones.
